Overview and definition
Microcontact printing (μCP), a core soft lithography technique, uses a microstructured elastomeric stamp to transfer “ink” molecules onto substrates by conformal contact, enabling direct or indirect patterning at micro and nanoscale dimensions without high vacuum or complex tooling.<cite id="3cf6ed03-0">Soft lithography is a micro-and nanoscale 3D structure fabrication technology that utilizes flexible materials (e.g., polymers or elastomers) as stamps to form micron-or nanoscale patterns on a substrate through physical contact or chemical interaction in a direct or indirect manner</cite><cite id="3cf6ed03-0">Microcontact printing (μCP), the most mature soft lithography process, is a method used for patterning molecular ink onto a surface with an elastic stamp</cite><cite id="3cf6ed03-2">The corresponding PDMS stamp can then be inked with a molecule and put in contact with a target surface to transfer the molecules into a patterned layer</cite>. μCP sits among contact-transfer soft lithography methods alongside microtransfer molding and capillary-assisted molding, offering low-cost, high-resolution patterning on planar and curved surfaces for electronics, microfluidics, biosensors, and optics.<cite id="3cf6ed03-0">Based on the basic concept, various soft lithography techniques have been developed, including contact transfer-based microcontact printing (μCP), contact transfer microtransfer molding (μTM), solvent-assisted capillary micromolding (SAMIM), and capillary micromolding techniques (MIMIC) that rely on capillary forces</cite><cite id="3cf6ed03-0">Soft lithography allows the fabrication of complex and high-resolution microstructures on non-planar substrates and is relatively simple to execute</cite><cite id="3cf6ed03-0">These techniques find extensive applications in microfluidic chips, biosensors, nanoelectronic devices, and optical components</cite>.

Materials, stamps, and the workflow
Workflows begin with masters (typically silicon with micro/nano patterns) to replicate PDMS stamps, which are then inked and pressed onto targets; unpatterned areas can be exposed to secondary coatings to create composite patterns.<cite id="3cf6ed03-2">Soft lithography emerged in the early 90's as a technique based on the use of an elastomer material named polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS)</cite><cite id="3cf6ed03-2">This polymer can be poured onto a silicon-based master with micro- or nanostructures to obtain a PDMS replication of the master's structures</cite><cite id="d01ab6fc-0">The PDMS stamp is prepared by fabricating it from a master (typically microfabricated in silicon) having relief structures in photoresist on its surface (for details, see ref.)</cite><cite id="d01ab6fc-0">The material of interest (e.g., an alkanethiol) is transferred from the PDMS stamp onto the substrate surface (e.g., gold or silver)</cite><cite id="d01ab6fc-0">The bare areas of substrate surface that the PDMS stamp has not touched can be exposed to another coating material (e.g., another kind of alkanethiol)</cite>. Typical inks include self-assembled monolayer precursors such as alkanethiols for gold/silver, with headgroups tuned to control wettability and bioactivity (e.g., -COOH, -NH2, or RGD peptides for cell adhesion).<cite id="d01ab6fc-0">Many of the studies involving the patterning of proteins and cells using microcontact printing have used selfassembled monolayers (SAMs) of alkanethiols on gold</cite><cite id="d01ab6fc-0">The alkanethiols have a sulfide as the anchor group and a variety of headgroups</cite><cite id="d01ab6fc-0">The binding of thiol to gold is very strong, resulting in a fairly stable surface</cite><cite id="d01ab6fc-0">The headgroup can greatly alter the hydrophobicity/hydrophilicity of the surface and protein and cell binding</cite>. Stamp fabrication often includes a silane treatment of masters to prevent PDMS adhesion, followed by curing PDMS (e.g., Sylgard 184 90/10 PDMS/initiator) and peeling to obtain stamp surfaces for inking.<cite id="d01ab6fc-4">The masters fabricated by photolithography were silanized using a fluorosilane for 1 h in a vacuum chamber to avoid adhesion of PDMS to the master</cite><cite id="d01ab6fc-4">A mixture containing 90% PDMS and 10% wt initiator (Sylgard 184) was mixed and degassed; the degassed solution was casted onto the silanized master and baked for 3 h at 65 °C; the PDMS was subsequently peeled off</cite>. Inking can be done by exposing the stamp surface to solution briefly (e.g., 30 s in 0.5 mg/mL alkanethiol in ethanol), followed by drying and conformal contact printing under light pressure; unpatterned areas then receive secondary treatments for passivation or protein immobilization.<cite id="d01ab6fc-1">Inking of the PDMS stamp was performed by placing a few drops of alkanethiol solution onto its patterned surface for 30 s; the stamp was then dried using a bellows air blower; immediately after inking, the stamp was placed onto the gold surface with manual pressure ensuring conformal and stable contact</cite><cite id="d01ab6fc-0">The bare areas not touched by the stamp can be exposed to another coating material (e.g., another alkanethiol) to complete bichromatic patterns</cite><cite id="d01ab6fc-4">For direct microcontact printing, stamps were incubated with fibronectin and pressed onto substrates; passivation was carried out with BSA</cite>.

Mechanisms: SAM formation and reactive μCP
μCP can deliver precise SAM masks on noble metals by transferring alkanethiols that protect patterned regions during etching, enabling transfer of the resist pattern into underlying metal layers.<cite id="d01ab6fc-0">The material of interest (e.g., an alkanethiol) is transferred from the PDMS stamp onto the substrate surface (e.g., gold or silver)</cite><cite id="d01ab6fc-3">The structured SAM acts as an etch mask during wet chemical etching and the pattern is transfer into the gold layer</cite>. Beyond passive masks, “reactive μCP” or microcontact chemistry uses localized surface reactions to covalently functionalize substrate groups introduced prior to printing, leveraging the stamp/substrate interface’s preorganization and high reagent concentration for near-quantitative yields under mild conditions.<cite id="d01ab6fc-2">Soon after its development, mCP evolved as a powerful tool to pattern functional reactive monolayers by means of the local chemical reaction between an ink transferred by the stamp and the functional groups introduced on the substrate; this process is called "reactive mCP" or microcontact chemistry</cite><cite id="d01ab6fc-2">Reactions induced by mCP allow for near-quantitative yield, mild reaction conditions, and short reaction times mainly due to the high degree of preorganization of the surface-immobilized reactant and the high local concentration of reagents at the stamp/substrate interface</cite>. μCP can generate SAM patterns spanning tens of nanometers to millimeters, and has been used to etch-protect microelectronics features by thiol-masked gold patterning.<cite id="d01ab6fc-2">Top-down methods including microcontact printing are commonly employed to generate patterns of SAMs with sizes ranging from tens of nanometers to millimeters</cite><cite id="d01ab6fc-2">Patterns of alkanethiols on gold were conveniently used as an etch-protecting layer for the fabrication of microstructures with potential application in microelectronics</cite>.

Resolution, fidelity, and process control
μCP achieves micron-scale and often submicron features depending on stamp resolution and transfer conditions. Large-area microstructuring has been demonstrated using 4-inch PDMS stamps patterned by UV-nanoimprint, enabling sub-micron replication on gold layers after SAM formation and etching.<cite id="d01ab6fc-3">Large area µm and sub-µm structuring of gold layers was demonstrated using 4″ PDMS stamps fabricated from photolithographic and UV-nanoimprint masters and used to print alkanethiols that form SAM etch masks</cite>. Stamp prestrain can be exploited to shrink microfeatures optically printed on soft elastomers (e.g., SU-8 on Ecoflex) by a known factor, enabling definition of 800 nm lines on rigid substrates via a two-step transfer process.<cite id="df68d5dd-3">Introducing the proposed fabrication process, we successfully achieved 800 nm line patterns via microcontact printing by using a stamp whose 800 nm features were obtained by shrinking a 2 mm photolithographic pattern using pre-strain of 3.0</cite>. Printing time and pressure significantly affect fidelity; minimizing time at atmospheric pressure can yield optimal channel width/spacing in alkanethiol μCP patterns, while extended times or higher pressures can deform features.<cite id="df68d5dd-2">Cost-effective microcontact printing channels of self-assembled monolayers of alkanethiol on gold were prepared; variations in printing time (30 s–60 min) and pressure (840–4200 Pa) were studied, with best resolution structures printed under minimal printing time at atmospheric pressure</cite>. μCP also enables cm-scale patterning on curved and planar surfaces with gentle, conformal contact, suitable for non-planar electronics substrates.<cite id="3cf6ed03-2">The flexibility of the PDMS stamp and the ability to achieve conformal contact between the stamp and the surface enables high-resolution patterning on both planar and non-planar surfaces; areas greater than 50 cm² have been patterned by microcontact printing</cite>.

Applications
- Surface functionalization and etch masks for metals: μCP of alkanethiols on Au/Ag yields SAMs that control protein adsorption and cell adhesion, and serve as precise etch masks for microfabrication.<cite id="d01ab6fc-0">The microcontact printing provides the patterning of self-assembled monolayers, and the resulting control over the adsorption of adhesive proteins facilitates the patterning of cells on substrates</cite><cite id="d01ab6fc-3">The structured SAM acts as an etch mask during wet chemical etching and the pattern is transfer into the gold layer</cite>.
- Biomedical and cell patterning: μCP is widely used to pattern proteins and ECM cues to direct cell behavior on curved or irregular tissue-engineering substrates where photolithography is impractical, with PDMS stamps repeatedly used for large-area, multicycle printing.<cite id="3cf6ed03-1">Microcontact printing is a method similar to image transfer used to pattern molecules on a surface for cell behavior and protein adsorption applications; PDMS stamps produced by replica molding are inked and transferred repeatedly for large areas and multiple copies</cite><cite id="3cf6ed03-1">Curved surfaces can also be used successfully due to the flexibility of PDMS while photolithography is not suitable for such surfaces</cite>. Direct printing of fibronectin and subsequent passivation (e.g., BSA) yields micropatterned cues controlling cell adhesion and morphology.<cite id="d01ab6fc-4">For direct microcontact printing, stamps were incubated with fibronectin and pressed onto substrates; passivation was carried out with BSA</cite>.
- Flexible and stretchable electronics: μCP deposits soft, conductive inks (e.g., liquid metals) with stamp printing or droplet successive deposition to realize arbitrary planar interconnects, including intersecting and closed-loop circuits; oxide layers help preserve deposited droplet shapes.<cite id="df68d5dd-1">Microcontact printing is an inexpensive and clean-room free technique for depositing soft and conductive inks; two primary methods pattern liquid metals: stamp printing (entire transfer) and successive droplet deposition; circuits with intersecting and closed-loop features are possible, aided by oxide-preserving shape</cite>. μCP is also used to define polymer-metal microstructures in hybrid microelectrode arrays and multilayer PDMS devices via aligned, bonded layers.<cite id="df68d5dd-4">A uniform PDMS mortar was achieved using a thin-film PDMS microcontact printing method and used for bonding each layer in a multilayer soft lithography process to fabricate a PDMS–parylene hybrid microelectrode array integrated into a multi-organ-on-a-chip</cite>.
- Hybrid photolithography–μCP flows: μCP can transfer photoresist patterns from elastomeric stamps to rigid substrates for downstream patterning, enabling integration with standard microfabrication.<cite id="df68d5dd-3">We spincoated the PR layer on top of this and defined the pattern on a prepared Si substrate by microcontact printing, exhibiting successfully defined PR pattern with a width of 4 mm; submicrometer PR patterns were achieved using an 800 nm line stamp pattern obtained via pre-strain shrinking</cite>.

Advantages and limitations
Key advantages include low cost and clean-room-free operation, compatibility with curved/non-planar substrates, gentle handling enabling bioentity retention, large-area patterning, rapid cycles, and simple alignment via backside methods or repeated stamp reuse.<cite id="3cf6ed03-0">Soft lithography provides cost benefits, particularly in low-volume or lab-scale applications, and allows fabrication of complex and high-resolution microstructures on non-planar substrates; high-resolution patterning at low cost is crucial for body-comfort electronics</cite><cite id="3cf6ed03-2">The major advantages of microcontact printing are gentle transfer without damaging bioentities, conformal contact on planar and non-planar surfaces, suitability for large-area micro- or nanopatterning, biocompatibility, speed, and low cost</cite><cite id="3cf6ed03-3">Microstructuring of conductive PDMS is achieved by microcontact printing; a micro fabricated printing mold transfers thin layers of conductive PDMS from a carrier to a glass slide</cite><cite id="df68d5dd-3">The quasi-opacity of Ecoex challenges top-view optical alignment; however, backside alignment methods widely adopted in photolithography address this</cite>. μCP also supports reactive patterning and gradient formation via selective chemistry and stamp-based spatial control.<cite id="d01ab6fc-2">mCP evolved as a powerful tool to pattern functional reactive monolayers by local chemical reaction; it enhances slow reactions with near-quantitative yields under mild conditions</cite><cite id="d01ab6fc-2">Microcontact printing, scanning probes, UV and ebeam lithographies are commonly employed to generate patterns of SAMs with sizes ranging from tens of nanometers to millimeters</cite>. Practical limitations include misregistration and alignment accuracy (often manual), challenges in stacking multiple layers and separating small-pitch microstructures in molding, and limited vertical aspect ratio transfer; stamp-fabrication cost/complexity and transfer thickness constraints also apply when only thin layers can be imprinted.<cite id="3cf6ed03-0">There are certain challenges associated with soft lithography; the low accuracy of alignment, which relies on manual operation, is an area that requires improvement; accurately stacking multiple layers in the fabrication of multilayer structures remains a challenge</cite><cite id="3cf6ed03-3">In the case of microcontact printing, a printing mold has to be fabricated and only thin layers of conductive PDMS can be transferred</cite>. For conductive elastomer systems, micromolding can damage masters and complicate removal of small features, whereas μCP avoids some of these substrate-abrasion issues but requires precise stamping and drying of inks to maintain fidelity.<cite id="3cf6ed03-3">During removal of excess polymer, the master mold is often damaged or scratched, and it is difficult to thoroughly separate small pitched microstructures</cite><cite id="d01ab6fc-1">Inking time, solvent evaporation, and conformal contact are critical; the stamp is manually placed onto the substrate surface with adhesive forces ensuring stable contact during printing</cite>.

Variants and recent advances
Stamp engineering expands μCP’s reach: pre-strained soft elastomeric stamps enable submicron definition on rigid substrates by shrinking microfeatures; reactive μCP creates covalent monolayers and gradients; and UV-nanoimprint masters with 4-inch scale replication support high-throughput large-area patterning of SAMs for downstream etching and device transfer.<cite id="df68d5dd-3">Introducing the proposed fabrication process, we successfully achieved 800 nm line patterns via microcontact printing by using a stamp whose 800 nm features were obtained by shrinking a 2 mm photolithographic pattern using pre-strain of 3.0</cite><cite id="d01ab6fc-2">Reactive mCP enables local chemical reaction between transferred ink and substrate functional groups with near-quantitative yields under mild conditions</cite><cite id="d01ab6fc-3">Large area µm and sub-µm structuring of gold layers was demonstrated using 4″ PDMS stamps fabricated from photolithographic and UV-nanoimprint masters</cite>. μCP also integrates with hybrid soft/biotronics processes, such as aligning PDMS layers via printed “mortar” regions to bond multilayer devices for organ-on-chip and flexible bioelectronics.<cite id="df68d5dd-4">A uniform PDMS mortar was achieved using a thin-film PDMS microcontact printing method and used for bonding each layer in multilayer soft lithography for a PDMS–parylene hybrid microelectrode array integrated into a multi-organ-on-a-chip</cite>.

When to use μCP vs. alternatives
μCP is attractive where conformal, gentle contact printing on curved or large-area substrates is needed, and where low cost, rapid iteration, and integration with PDMS-based devices or soft electronics are priorities; it is widely used to mask metals for etching, to present controlled biofunctional surfaces, and to deposit soft conductors for stretchable circuits.<cite id="3cf6ed03-0">Soft lithography allows the fabrication of complex and high-resolution microstructures on non-planar substrates and is relatively simple to execute</cite><cite id="3cf6ed03-0">These techniques find extensive applications in microfluidic chips, biosensors, nanoelectronic devices, and optical components</cite><cite id="d01ab6fc-3">Structured SAMs printed by μCP act as etch masks to transfer patterns into gold layers</cite><cite id="df68d5dd-1">Microcontact printing is an inexpensive and clean-room free technique for depositing soft and conductive inks and can pattern liquid metals into arbitrary planar interconnects</cite>. For high-throughput photolithographic layers, μCP is often combined with standard resist processing to transfer microfeature patterns before development/etching; for truly high-aspect or multilayer microelectronics, μCP provides a complementary, gentle approach to define features and interfaces that can be completed by downstream hard-bonding steps.<cite id="df68d5dd-3">Spincoating a photoresist on a μCP-defined elastomeric stamp and contacting it to a substrate defined PR patterns down to 800 nm, then proceeding with standard microfabrication</cite><cite id="3cf6ed03-0">Soft lithography offers significant advantages for flexible electronics fabrication, including cost benefits and fabrication on non-planar substrates</cite>.

Practical notes and recipes
- Stamp making: Silanize a photolithographic master (e.g., fluorosilane) to reduce PDMS adhesion; mix 90% PDMS/10% Sylgard 184 (or equivalent), degas, cast on the master, cure 65 °C for ~3 h, and peel to obtain a PDMS stamp with microfeatures; optionally coat stamp backsides for handling.<cite id="d01ab6fc-4">Masters were silanized for 1 h; PDMS/Sylgard 90/10 was degassed, cast, and baked 3 h at 65 °C; PDMS was peeled off</cite>.
- Inking and printing: Immerse stamp features in 0.5 mg/mL alkanethiol (e.g., HS-(CH2)15-COOH, HS-(CH2)16-NH2, HS-(CH2)15-CH3) in ethanol for ~30 s; dry with a gentle blower; place stamp on clean Au/Si (50 nm Au on Si) with light manual pressure to ensure conformal contact; lift to transfer SAMs.<cite id="d01ab6fc-1">Inking for 30 s in 0.5 mg/mL alkanethiol in ethanol, drying, and conformal contact printing on Au/Si with manual pressure</cite>.
- Masking and etch transfer: Patterned SAMs resist wet etching to transfer features into underlying metal layers; unmasked regions are etched away, leaving μCP-defined metal features.<cite id="d01ab6fc-3">The structured SAM acts as an etch mask during wet chemical etching and the pattern is transfer into the gold layer</cite>.
- Fidelity control: Keep printing times short and pressures modest for micron-scale channels to avoid deformation; verify stamp feature size and substrate contact with optical/MRI alignment and backside registration strategies.<cite id="df68d5dd-2">Minimal printing time at atmospheric pressure produced best resolution in channel patterns</cite><cite id="df68d5dd-3">Backside alignment methods are commonly used when stamps are optically quasi-transparent</cite>.
- Biofunctionalization: After SAM printing, incubate with ECM proteins (e.g., fibronectin) to promote cell adhesion on patterned islands; passivate unpatterned areas (e.g., BSA) to suppress nonspecific binding.<cite id="d01ab6fc-4">Stamps incubated with fibronectin and pressed onto substrates; passivation with BSA</cite><cite id="d01ab6fc-0">RGD peptide headgroups promote cell attachment and can replace conventional passivation chemistries</cite>.
- Stretchable interconnects: Use μCP stamp transfer or successive droplet deposition to pattern liquid-metal lines on elastomeric carriers; oxidation layers stabilize deposited features during circuit formation.<cite id="df68d5dd-1">Stamp printing and successive droplet deposition of liquid metal enable arbitrary planar patterns including intersecting and closed-loop circuits; oxide layers preserve deposited droplet shapes</cite>.

Summary
Microcontact printing is a robust, low-cost, and conformal soft-lithography method that transfers molecular inks—most notably alkanethiols to form SAM masks and biofunctional interfaces—from PDMS stamps to substrates, enabling micron-to-submicron patterning on planar and curved surfaces for electronics, photonics, microfluidics, and bioelectronics.<cite id="3cf6ed03-0">Soft lithography and its contact-transfer μCP method enable high-resolution microstructures on curved and planar substrates for flexible electronics, microfluidics, biosensors, and optics</cite><cite id="d01ab6fc-0">μCP transfers alkanethiols from PDMS stamps to Au/Ag to pattern SAMs that control protein adsorption and cells, and serve as etch-protective masks</cite><cite id="3cf6ed03-2">PDMS stamps replicated from masters are inked and contacted to transfer molecules into patterned layers; the technique is attractive because of simplicity, biocompatibility, speed, and low cost</cite>. While alignment, multilayer stacking, and stamp-feature transfer fidelity remain practical challenges, stamp engineering, reactive chemistry, and integration with standard microfabrication and soft-biointerface workflows have broadened μCP’s utility across devices from stretchable interconnects to organ-on-chip interfaces.<cite id="3cf6ed03-0">Soft lithography faces alignment accuracy and multilayer stacking challenges that require improvement</cite><cite id="df68d5dd-3">Pre-strained elastomeric stamps enable 800 nm pattern transfer via two-step μCP</cite><cite id="df68d5dd-1">μCP enables clean-room free deposition of liquid metals for complex interconnect patterns</cite><cite id="df68d5dd-4">Thin-film microcontact printed PDMS layers bond multilayer structures in PDMS–parylene devices for organ-on-chip integration</cite>.

Title: Revolutionizing wearable technology: advanced fabrication techniques for body-conformable electronics
Snippet: Soft lithography is a micro-and nanoscale 3D structure fabrication technology that utilizes flexible materials (e.g., polymers or elastomers) as stamps to form micron-or nanoscale patterns on a substrate through physical contact or chemical interaction in a direct or indirect manner 87,88 . Based on the basic concept, various soft lithography techniques have been developed, including contact transfer-based microcontact printing (μCP), contact transfer microtransfer molding (μTM), solvent-assisted capillary micromolding (SAMIM), and capillary micromolding techniques (MIMIC) that rely on capillary forces. These techniques are widely used for fabricating 3D structures. Soft lithography offers significant advantages for flexible electronics fabrication. It provides cost benefits, particularly in low-volume or lab-scale applications. Moreover, soft lithography allows the fabrication of complex and high-resolution microstructures on non-planar substrates and is relatively simple to execute. The realization of high-resolution patterning at low cost is crucial for the further development of body-comfort electronics. These technologies find extensive applications in microfluidic chips, biosensors, nanoelectronic devices, and optical components 89 . However, there are certain challenges associated with soft lithography that need to be addressed. The low accuracy of alignment, which relies on manual operation, is an area that requires improvement. Additionally, accurately stacking multiple layers in the fabrication of multilayer structures remains a challenge that needs to be overcome in this technology. Soft lithography technology has unveiled significant potential and prospective applications within the micro-and nano-manufacturing domain. In biomedical applications, the deployment of flexible biosensors and microfluidic devices is anticipated to catalyze the evolution of personalized healthcare and the proliferation of point-of-care diagnostic methodologies. 

Microcontact printing (μCP) μCP, the most mature soft lithography process, is a method used for patterning molecular ink onto a surface with an elastic stamp. In this process, the desired molecules such as metals and nanoparticles are applied to the stamp, which is then brought into conformal contact with the substrate.
</snippet>

Title: Micro and Nanofabrication methods to control cell-substrate interactions and cell behavior: A review from the tissue engineering perspective
Snippet: Micro and nanostructures can be constructed using soft lithography and employ polymers such as polydimethylsiloxane, PDMS as templates (soft lithography) or stamps (microcontact printing) (Fig. 2cee). Soft lithography has the advantages of low cost and ease and is frequently used in the production of micropatterned substrates from various materials [16,58,60,67,68]. Curved surfaces can also be used successfully due to the flexibility of PDMS while photolithography is not suitable for such surfaces [69]. Microcontact printing is a method similar to image transfer like a regular stamp and ink. It is used to pattern molecules on a surface for cell behavior and protein adsorption applications [61,62]. In microcontact printing, PDMS is used to produce a stamp by replica molding. Then the stamp is inked to adsorb cells, proteins and other molecules to transfer them onto the substrate. After the stamp is pressed, the solvent is evaporated, and molecules are transferred, the stamp is removed revealing the patterns. Microcontact printing can be used for large areas, and multiple copies of the patterns can be obtained by a single stamp by applying it repeatedly. High aspect ratio patterns is not possible with this technique.
</snippet>

Title: Soft Lithography, a Tool to Address Single-Objects Investigations
Snippet: Soft-lithography emerged in the early 90's as a technique based on the use of an elastomer material named polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS). This polymer can be poured onto a siliconbased master with micro-or nanostructures made by photolithography or electron beam lithography respectively, to obtain a PDMS replication of the master's structures. The corresponding PDMS stamp can then be inked with a molecule and put in contact with a target surface to transfer the molecules into a patterned layer. This is what we call microcontact printing (Kumar & Whitesides, 1993;Xia & Whitesides, 1998). The major advantages of microcontact printing are that the contact with the surface is made in a very gentle manner, so the bioentities are transferred without damaging them. The flexibility of the PDMS stamp and the ability to achieve conformal contact between the stamp and the surface enables high-resolution patterning on both planar and non-planar surfaces. Areas greater than 50 cm² have been patterned by microcontact printing (Xia et al., 1996). So this technique is suitable for large-area micro-or nanopatterning, and is attractive because of its simplicity, biocompatibility, speed, and low cost. Directed Capillary Assembly is another interesting technique that has received constant interest throughout the years. This technique was first introduced by Denkov et al. in the 90's. At that time, their objective was to produce photonic band gap materials based on the compact assembly of dielectric colloids (silica beads). The method relied on the direct evaporation of a droplet of a colloidal solution on a surface and was called Capillary Force Assembly (CFA). The nanoparticles dragged by the convective flux in the droplet were forced to assemble on the surface close to the liquid meniscus. A few years later, the group of Alivisatos (Klein et al., 1996) showed how this method could be combined with topographic patterns in order to control the position of the assembly as well as the shape of the nanoparticles' patterns and this was called "Lithography Guided Capillary Force Assembly".
</snippet>

Title: Highly elastic conductive polymeric MEMS
Snippet: To show the feasibility of the process, we prepared different mixtures of conductive particles added to a very soft PDMS base material. Conductivity is attained by use of carbon black powder, MWCNTs, and silver flakes. However, to achieve conductivity, various other admixtures are conceivable and do not impair the fabrication process itself. The electrical properties of these three different mixtures are measured with a special focus on conductivity under strain. As a possible application for the process, we finally fabricated a highly elastic strain gauge, and we showed the results of the electrical measurements under high strain.

Microstructuring of conductive PDMS is achieved by micromolding, where a negative mold of the desired structure is used to define the geometry of the polymer. This negative mold is frequently made of a thick film resist coated on a silicon or glass substrate. Alternatively, molding microstructures directly etched into silicon or glass is the method of choice. In both cases, conductive PDMS is poured onto the micromold and excess composite is scraped off using a blade or a similar tool. Nonconductive PDMS is then poured on top of the conductive PDMS as an insulating carrier layer. After cross-linking, the PDMS carrier layer can be peeled off the mold, along with the conductive layer. This method is often referred to as soft lithography. Another way to pattern conductive PDMS is microcontact printing. In this case, a micro fabricated printing mold (e.g., poly(methyl methacrylate)), is used to transfer a thin layer of conductive PDMS from a carrier to a glass slide. In a subsequent step, nonconductive PDMS is poured on top of the imprinted conductive PDMS. After curing, the PDMS layer can again be peeled off, along with the printed microstructures.

Both micromolding approaches, either by using structured resist or etched structures in a substrate, have their downsides. During removal of excess polymer, the master mold is often damaged or scratched, and it is difficult to thoroughly separate small pitched microstructures. In the case of microcontact printing, a printing mold has to be fabricated and only thin layers of conductive PDMS can be transferred
</snippet>

In this process, a uniform PDMS mortar (uncured PDMS) was achieved using a thin-film PDMS microcontact printing method 66,67) and was used for bonding each layer. Title: Nanofabrication of Nonfouling Surfaces for Micropatterning of Cell and Microtissue
Snippet: The microcontact printing method [108,109] is based on the pattern transfer of the material of interest from the PDMS stamp onto the substrate surface. The PDMS stamp is prepared by fabricating it from a master (typically microfabricated in silicon) having relief structures in photoresist on its surface (for details, see ref. [105]). Photolithography is used for the fabrication of masters in preparing PDMS stamps. Many of the studies involving the patterning of proteins and cells using microcontact printing have used selfassembled monolayers (SAMs) of alkanethiols on gold. As shown in Figure 10(b), the material of interest (e.g., an alkanethiol) is transferred from the PDMS stamp onto the substrate surface (e.g., gold or silver). The bare areas of substrate surface that the PDMS stamp has not touched can be exposed to another coating material (e.g., another kind of alkanethiol). The microcontact printing provides the patterning of self-assembled monolayers, and the resulting control over the adsorption of adhesive proteins facilitates the patterning of cells on substrates [108][109][110][111][112]. 

Chemicals to form SAMs typically have a chemical formula of Y(CH 2 )nX where Y is the anchor and X is the headgroup. The nature of the monolayer including its ability to self-assemble is influenced by n, or the number of methyl residues. The alkanethiols have a sulfide as the anchor group and a variety of headgroups. The binding of thiol to gold is very strong, resulting in a fairly stable surface. Typical headgroups are CH 3 or COOH. The headgroup can greatly alter the hydrophobicity/hydrophilicity of the surface and protein and cell binding. The headgroup can be modified chemically. For example, an arginine-glycine-aspartate (RGD) peptide can be used as a headgroup that promotes cell attachment.
</snippet>

Title: Reactive self-assembled monolayers: from surface functionalization to gradient formation
Snippet: nucleophilic substitutions, [17][18][19] esterication, 20 amidation, 21-23 etc.). 

In the last decade a lot of effort was focused on the implementation of methods to obtain selective, efficient, robust, quantitative, simple and rapid surface transformations to reduce the formation of by-products, avoiding the need for purication and allowing easy surface analysis. Click chemistry encompasses all these properties. ][28][29][30][31] Microcontact printing (mCP), scanning probes, UV and ebeam lithographies, the so-called "top-down" methods, are commonly employed to generate patterns of SAMs with sizes ranging from tens of nanometers to millimeters. 3][34] In the conventional mCP, a microstructured elastomeric poly(dimethylsiloxane) (PDMS) stamp was employed to transfer molecules of the "ink" (e.g. thiols) to the surface of the substrate (e.g. gold) by conformal contact. Patterns of alkanethiols on gold were conveniently used as an etch-protecting layer for the fabrication of microstructures with potential application in microelectronics. 

Soon aer its development, mCP evolved as a powerful tool to pattern functional reactive monolayers by means of the local chemical reaction between an ink transferred by the stamp and the functional groups introduced on the substrate. This process is called "reactive mCP" or microcontact chemistry [35][36][37] (Scheme 2). 

mCP is an efficient method, and enhances slow and uncatalyzed reactions at the interface. 36 Reactions induced by mCP allow for near-quantitative yield, mild reaction conditions, and short reaction times, mainly due to the high degree of preorganization of the surface-immobilized reactant and the high local concentration of reagents (ink) at the stamp/substrate interface. 

Surface gradients are surfaces with a gradual variation of at least one physicochemical property in space that may evolve in time.

Title: Large area μm and sub-μm structuring of gold layers with microcontact printing using 4″ and 1″ PDMS stamps
Snippet: Microcontact printing (µCP) is a simple yet excellent method to functionalize surfaces by using a structured elastomeric stamp to transfer patterns of the desired substances directly onto the substrate surface. µCP of alkanethiols on gold was the first representative of soft-lithography processes [1]. The principle of µCP is schematically shown in figure 1. 

One of the key elements of µCP is the stamp made of poly(dimethylsiloxane) (PDMS) which is the negative copy of a master. In this work the stamp was used for printing alkanethiols onto a gold surface which form a self-assembled monolayer (SAM) on gold. The structured SAM acts as an etch mask during wet chemical etching and the pattern is transfer into the gold layer. 

We fabricated PDMS stamps directly on a rigid glass back-plate. As masters we used 4" Si wafers structured by photolithography and 1" masters structured by UV-nanoimprint lithography (UV-NIL). Large area µm and sub-µm structuring of gold layers was demonstrated using these 4" and 1" PDMS stamps.
</snippet>

Title: Robust and Multifunctional Liquid-Metal Embedded Elastomers for Ultrastretchable Electronics: a Short Review
Snippet: Microcontact printing is an inexpensive and clean-room free technique for depositing soft and conductive inks on a soft substrate. There are two primary methods to pattern liquid metals using micro-contact printing: 1-Stamp printing or entire transferring of ink using a topographical stamp, and 2-successive deposition of individual droplets of liquid metal with a hemispherical print head. In contrast to stencil lithography and injecting filling, microcontact printing (stamp printing and successive deposition) can be used to create circuits with any planar pattern with intersecting and closed-loop circuit features [28,34]. 

The process benefits from the oxide layer, which preserves the shape of the deposited droplets of liquid metal.
</snippet>

Title: Time and pressure dependent deformation of microcontact printed channels fabricated using self-assembled monolayers of alkanethiol on gold
Snippet: Abstract In this work, the replication-based microcontact printing method has been presented to study the deformation effect of different printing times and printing pressures on the microcontact printed structures. Cost-effective microcontact printing channels of self-assembled monolayers of alkanethiol have been prepared on gold surface. The alkanethiol inking the polydimethylsiloxanes stamp effectively forms the self-assembled monolayers on the noble gold surface that protects the metal against etchant solution and thereby forms channel-like structures. To address the deformation issue, variations in the printing time in the range of 30 s–60 min and the printing pressure ranging from 840 to 4200 Pa have been studied. The estimation of differing the channel width and channel space with varying printing time and pressure shows the best resolution structures printed under minimal printing time at atmospheric pressure.
</snippet>

Overview and definition
Microcontact printing (μCP), a core soft lithography technique, uses a microstructured elastomeric stamp to transfer “ink” molecules onto substrates by conformal contact, enabling direct or indirect patterning at micro and nanoscale dimensions without high vacuum or complex tooling.<cite id="3cf6ed03-0">Soft lithography is a micro-and nanoscale 3D structure fabrication technology that utilizes flexible materials (e.g., polymers or elastomers) as stamps to form micron-or nanoscale patterns on a substrate through physical contact or chemical interaction in a direct or indirect manner</cite><cite id="3cf6ed03-0">Microcontact printing (μCP), the most mature soft lithography process, is a method used for patterning molecular ink onto a surface with an elastic stamp</cite><cite id="3cf6ed03-2">The corresponding PDMS stamp can then be inked with a molecule and put in contact with a target surface to transfer the molecules into a patterned layer</cite>. μCP sits among contact-transfer soft lithography methods alongside microtransfer molding and capillary-assisted molding, offering low-cost, high-resolution patterning on planar and curved surfaces for electronics, microfluidics, biosensors, and optics.<cite id="3cf6ed03-0">Based on the basic concept, various soft lithography techniques have been developed, including contact transfer-based microcontact printing (μCP), contact transfer microtransfer molding (μTM), solvent-assisted capillary micromolding (SAMIM), and capillary micromolding techniques (MIMIC) that rely on capillary forces</cite><cite id="3cf6ed03-0">Soft lithography allows the fabrication of complex and high-resolution microstructures on non-planar substrates and is relatively simple to execute</cite><cite id="3cf6ed03-0">These techniques find extensive applications in microfluidic chips, biosensors, nanoelectronic devices, and optical components</cite>.

Materials, stamps, and the workflow
Workflows begin with masters (typically silicon with micro/nano patterns) to replicate PDMS stamps, which are then inked and pressed onto targets; unpatterned areas can be exposed to secondary coatings to create composite patterns.<cite id="3cf6ed03-2">Soft lithography emerged in the early 90's as a technique based on the use of an elastomer material named polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS)</cite><cite id="3cf6ed03-2">This polymer can be poured onto a silicon-based master with micro- or nanostructures to obtain a PDMS replication of the master's structures</cite><cite id="d01ab6fc-0">The PDMS stamp is prepared by fabricating it from a master (typically microfabricated in silicon) having relief structures in photoresist on its surface (for details, see ref.)</cite><cite id="d01ab6fc-0">The material of interest (e.g., an alkanethiol) is transferred from the PDMS stamp onto the substrate surface (e.g., gold or silver)</cite><cite id="d01ab6fc-0">The bare areas of substrate surface that the PDMS stamp has not touched can be exposed to another coating material (e.g., another kind of alkanethiol)</cite>. Typical inks include self-assembled monolayer precursors such as alkanethiols for gold/silver, with headgroups tuned to control wettability and bioactivity (e.g., -COOH, -NH2, or RGD peptides for cell adhesion).<cite id="d01ab6fc-0">Many of the studies involving the patterning of proteins and cells using microcontact printing have used selfassembled monolayers (SAMs) of alkanethiols on gold</cite><cite id="d01ab6fc-0">The alkanethiols have a sulfide as the anchor group and a variety of headgroups</cite><cite id="d01ab6fc-0">The binding of thiol to gold is very strong, resulting in a fairly stable surface</cite><cite id="d01ab6fc-0">The headgroup can greatly alter the hydrophobicity/hydrophilicity of the surface and protein and cell binding</cite>. Stamp fabrication often includes a silane treatment of masters to prevent PDMS adhesion, followed by curing PDMS (e.g., Sylgard 184 90/10 PDMS/initiator) and peeling to obtain stamp surfaces for inking.<cite id="d01ab6fc-4">The masters fabricated by photolithography were silanized using a fluorosilane for 1 h in a vacuum chamber to avoid adhesion of PDMS to the master</cite><cite id="d01ab6fc-4">A mixture containing 90% PDMS and 10% wt initiator (Sylgard 184) was mixed and degassed; the degassed solution was casted onto the silanized master and baked for 3 h at 65 °C; the PDMS was subsequently peeled off</cite>. Inking can be done by exposing the stamp surface to solution briefly (e.g., 30 s in 0.5 mg/mL alkanethiol in ethanol), followed by drying and conformal contact printing under light pressure; unpatterned areas then receive secondary treatments for passivation or protein immobilization.<cite id="d01ab6fc-1">Inking of the PDMS stamp was performed by placing a few drops of alkanethiol solution onto its patterned surface for 30 s; the stamp was then dried using a bellows air blower; immediately after inking, the stamp was placed onto the gold surface with manual pressure ensuring conformal and stable contact</cite><cite id="d01ab6fc-0">The bare areas not touched by the stamp can be exposed to another coating material (e.g., another alkanethiol) to complete bichromatic patterns</cite><cite id="d01ab6fc-4">For direct microcontact printing, stamps were incubated with fibronectin and pressed onto substrates; passivation was carried out with BSA</cite>.

Mechanisms: SAM formation and reactive μCP
μCP can deliver precise SAM masks on noble metals by transferring alkanethiols that protect patterned regions during etching, enabling transfer of the resist pattern into underlying metal layers.<cite id="d01ab6fc-0">The material of interest (e.g., an alkanethiol) is transferred from the PDMS stamp onto the substrate surface (e.g., gold or silver)</cite><cite id="d01ab6fc-3">The structured SAM acts as an etch mask during wet chemical etching and the pattern is transfer into the gold layer</cite>. Beyond passive masks, “reactive μCP” or microcontact chemistry uses localized surface reactions to covalently functionalize substrate groups introduced prior to printing, leveraging the stamp/substrate interface’s preorganization and high reagent concentration for near-quantitative yields under mild conditions.<cite id="d01ab6fc-2">Soon after its development, mCP evolved as a powerful tool to pattern functional reactive monolayers by means of the local chemical reaction between an ink transferred by the stamp and the functional groups introduced on the substrate; this process is called "reactive mCP" or microcontact chemistry</cite><cite id="d01ab6fc-2">Reactions induced by mCP allow for near-quantitative yield, mild reaction conditions, and short reaction times mainly due to the high degree of preorganization of the surface-immobilized reactant and the high local concentration of reagents at the stamp/substrate interface</cite>. μCP can generate SAM patterns spanning tens of nanometers to millimeters, and has been used to etch-protect microelectronics features by thiol-masked gold patterning.<cite id="d01ab6fc-2">Top-down methods including microcontact printing are commonly employed to generate patterns of SAMs with sizes ranging from tens of nanometers to millimeters</cite><cite id="d01ab6fc-2">Patterns of alkanethiols on gold were conveniently used as an etch-protecting layer for the fabrication of microstructures with potential application in microelectronics</cite>.

Resolution, fidelity, and process control
μCP achieves micron-scale and often submicron features depending on stamp resolution and transfer conditions. Large-area microstructuring has been demonstrated using 4-inch PDMS stamps patterned by UV-nanoimprint, enabling sub-micron replication on gold layers after SAM formation and etching.<cite id="d01ab6fc-3">Large area µm and sub-µm structuring of gold layers was demonstrated using 4″ PDMS stamps fabricated from photolithographic and UV-nanoimprint masters and used to print alkanethiols that form SAM etch masks</cite>. Stamp prestrain can be exploited to shrink microfeatures optically printed on soft elastomers (e.g., SU-8 on Ecoflex) by a known factor, enabling definition of 800 nm lines on rigid substrates via a two-step transfer process.<cite id="df68d5dd-3">Introducing the proposed fabrication process, we successfully achieved 800 nm line patterns via microcontact printing by using a stamp whose 800 nm features were obtained by shrinking a 2 mm photolithographic pattern using pre-strain of 3.0</cite>. Printing time and pressure significantly affect fidelity; minimizing time at atmospheric pressure can yield optimal channel width/spacing in alkanethiol μCP patterns, while extended times or higher pressures can deform features.<cite id="df68d5dd-2">Cost-effective microcontact printing channels of self-assembled monolayers of alkanethiol on gold were prepared; variations in printing time (30 s–60 min) and pressure (840–4200 Pa) were studied, with best resolution structures printed under minimal printing time at atmospheric pressure</cite>. μCP also enables cm-scale patterning on curved and planar surfaces with gentle, conformal contact, suitable for non-planar electronics substrates.<cite id="3cf6ed03-2">The flexibility of the PDMS stamp and the ability to achieve conformal contact between the stamp and the surface enables high-resolution patterning on both planar and non-planar surfaces; areas greater than 50 cm² have been patterned by microcontact printing</cite>.

Applications
- Surface functionalization and etch masks for metals: μCP of alkanethiols on Au/Ag yields SAMs that control protein adsorption and cell adhesion, and serve as precise etch masks for microfabrication.<cite id="d01ab6fc-0">The microcontact printing provides the patterning of self-assembled monolayers, and the resulting control over the adsorption of adhesive proteins facilitates the patterning of cells on substrates</cite><cite id="d01ab6fc-3">The structured SAM acts as an etch mask during wet chemical etching and the pattern is transfer into the gold layer</cite>.
- Biomedical and cell patterning: μCP is widely used to pattern proteins and ECM cues to direct cell behavior on curved or irregular tissue-engineering substrates where photolithography is impractical, with PDMS stamps repeatedly used for large-area, multicycle printing.<cite id="3cf6ed03-1">Microcontact printing is a method similar to image transfer used to pattern molecules on a surface for cell behavior and protein adsorption applications; PDMS stamps produced by replica molding are inked and transferred repeatedly for large areas and multiple copies</cite><cite id="3cf6ed03-1">Curved surfaces can also be used successfully due to the flexibility of PDMS while photolithography is not suitable for such surfaces</cite>. Direct printing of fibronectin and subsequent passivation (e.g., BSA) yields micropatterned cues controlling cell adhesion and morphology.<cite id="d01ab6fc-4">For direct microcontact printing, stamps were incubated with fibronectin and pressed onto substrates; passivation was carried out with BSA</cite>.
- Flexible and stretchable electronics: μCP deposits soft, conductive inks (e.g., liquid metals) with stamp printing or droplet successive deposition to realize arbitrary planar interconnects, including intersecting and closed-loop circuits; oxide layers help preserve deposited droplet shapes.<cite id="df68d5dd-1">Microcontact printing is an inexpensive and clean-room free technique for depositing soft and conductive inks; two primary methods pattern liquid metals: stamp printing (entire transfer) and successive droplet deposition; circuits with intersecting and closed-loop features are possible, aided by oxide-preserving shape</cite>. μCP is also used to define polymer-metal microstructures in hybrid microelectrode arrays and multilayer PDMS devices via aligned, bonded layers.<cite id="df68d5dd-4">A uniform PDMS mortar was achieved using a thin-film PDMS microcontact printing method and used for bonding each layer in a multilayer soft lithography process to fabricate a PDMS–parylene hybrid microelectrode array integrated into a multi-organ-on-a-chip</cite>.
- Hybrid photolithography–μCP flows: μCP can transfer photoresist patterns from elastomeric stamps to rigid substrates for downstream patterning, enabling integration with standard microfabrication.<cite id="df68d5dd-3">We spincoated the PR layer on top of this and defined the pattern on a prepared Si substrate by microcontact printing, exhibiting successfully defined PR pattern with a width of 4 mm; submicrometer PR patterns were achieved using an 800 nm line stamp pattern obtained via pre-strain shrinking</cite>.

Advantages and limitations
Key advantages include low cost and clean-room-free operation, compatibility with curved/non-planar substrates, gentle handling enabling bioentity retention, large-area patterning, rapid cycles, and simple alignment via backside methods or repeated stamp reuse.<cite id="3cf6ed03-0">Soft lithography provides cost benefits, particularly in low-volume or lab-scale applications, and allows fabrication of complex and high-resolution microstructures on non-planar substrates; high-resolution patterning at low cost is crucial for body-comfort electronics</cite><cite id="3cf6ed03-2">The major advantages of microcontact printing are gentle transfer without damaging bioentities, conformal contact on planar and non-planar surfaces, suitability for large-area micro- or nanopatterning, biocompatibility, speed, and low cost</cite><cite id="3cf6ed03-3">Microstructuring of conductive PDMS is achieved by microcontact printing; a micro fabricated printing mold transfers thin layers of conductive PDMS from a carrier to a glass slide</cite><cite id="df68d5dd-3">The quasi-opacity of Ecoex challenges top-view optical alignment; however, backside alignment methods widely adopted in photolithography address this</cite>. μCP also supports reactive patterning and gradient formation via selective chemistry and stamp-based spatial control.<cite id="d01ab6fc-2">mCP evolved as a powerful tool to pattern functional reactive monolayers by local chemical reaction; it enhances slow reactions with near-quantitative yields under mild conditions</cite><cite id="d01ab6fc-2">Microcontact printing, scanning probes, UV and ebeam lithographies are commonly employed to generate patterns of SAMs with sizes ranging from tens of nanometers to millimeters</cite>. Practical limitations include misregistration and alignment accuracy (often manual), challenges in stacking multiple layers and separating small-pitch microstructures in molding, and limited vertical aspect ratio transfer; stamp-fabrication cost/complexity and transfer thickness constraints also apply when only thin layers can be imprinted.<cite id="3cf6ed03-0">There are certain challenges associated with soft lithography; the low accuracy of alignment, which relies on manual operation, is an area that requires improvement; accurately stacking multiple layers in the fabrication of multilayer structures remains a challenge</cite><cite id="3cf6ed03-3">In the case of microcontact printing, a printing mold has to be fabricated and only thin layers of conductive PDMS can be transferred</cite>. For conductive elastomer systems, micromolding can damage masters and complicate removal of small features, whereas μCP avoids some of these substrate-abrasion issues but requires precise stamping and drying of inks to maintain fidelity.<cite id="3cf6ed03-3">During removal of excess polymer, the master mold is often damaged or scratched, and it is difficult to thoroughly separate small pitched microstructures</cite><cite id="d01ab6fc-1">Inking time, solvent evaporation, and conformal contact are critical; the stamp is manually placed onto the substrate surface with adhesive forces ensuring stable contact during printing</cite>.

Variants and recent advances
Stamp engineering expands μCP’s reach: pre-strained soft elastomeric stamps enable submicron definition on rigid substrates by shrinking microfeatures; reactive μCP creates covalent monolayers and gradients; and UV-nanoimprint masters with 4-inch scale replication support high-throughput large-area patterning of SAMs for downstream etching and device transfer.<cite id="df68d5dd-3">Introducing the proposed fabrication process, we successfully achieved 800 nm line patterns via microcontact printing by using a stamp whose 800 nm features were obtained by shrinking a 2 mm photolithographic pattern using pre-strain of 3.0</cite><cite id="d01ab6fc-2">Reactive mCP enables local chemical reaction between transferred ink and substrate functional groups with near-quantitative yields under mild conditions</cite><cite id="d01ab6fc-3">Large area µm and sub-µm structuring of gold layers was demonstrated using 4″ PDMS stamps fabricated from photolithographic and UV-nanoimprint masters</cite>. μCP also integrates with hybrid soft/biotronics processes, such as aligning PDMS layers via printed “mortar” regions to bond multilayer devices for organ-on-chip and flexible bioelectronics.<cite id="df68d5dd-4">A uniform PDMS mortar was achieved using a thin-film PDMS microcontact printing method and used for bonding each layer in multilayer soft lithography for a PDMS–parylene hybrid microelectrode array integrated into a multi-organ-on-a-chip</cite>.

When to use μCP vs. alternatives
μCP is attractive where conformal, gentle contact printing on curved or large-area substrates is needed, and where low cost, rapid iteration, and integration with PDMS-based devices or soft electronics are priorities; it is widely used to mask metals for etching, to present controlled biofunctional surfaces, and to deposit soft conductors for stretchable circuits.<cite id="3cf6ed03-0">Soft lithography allows the fabrication of complex and high-resolution microstructures on non-planar substrates and is relatively simple to execute</cite><cite id="3cf6ed03-0">These techniques find extensive applications in microfluidic chips, biosensors, nanoelectronic devices, and optical components</cite><cite id="d01ab6fc-3">Structured SAMs printed by μCP act as etch masks to transfer patterns into gold layers</cite><cite id="df68d5dd-1">Microcontact printing is an inexpensive and clean-room free technique for depositing soft and conductive inks and can pattern liquid metals into arbitrary planar interconnects</cite>. For high-throughput photolithographic layers, μCP is often combined with standard resist processing to transfer microfeature patterns before development/etching; for truly high-aspect or multilayer microelectronics, μCP provides a complementary, gentle approach to define features and interfaces that can be completed by downstream hard-bonding steps.<cite id="df68d5dd-3">Spincoating a photoresist on a μCP-defined elastomeric stamp and contacting it to a substrate defined PR patterns down to 800 nm, then proceeding with standard microfabrication</cite><cite id="3cf6ed03-0">Soft lithography offers significant advantages for flexible electronics fabrication, including cost benefits and fabrication on non-planar substrates</cite>.

Practical notes and recipes
- Stamp making: Silanize a photolithographic master (e.g., fluorosilane) to reduce PDMS adhesion; mix 90% PDMS/10% Sylgard 184 (or equivalent), degas, cast on the master, cure 65 °C for ~3 h, and peel to obtain a PDMS stamp with microfeatures; optionally coat stamp backsides for handling.<cite id="d01ab6fc-4">Masters were silanized for 1 h; PDMS/Sylgard 90/10 was degassed, cast, and baked 3 h at 65 °C; PDMS was peeled off</cite>.
- Inking and printing: Immerse stamp features in 0.5 mg/mL alkanethiol (e.g., HS-(CH2)15-COOH, HS-(CH2)16-NH2, HS-(CH2)15-CH3) in ethanol for ~30 s; dry with a gentle blower; place stamp on clean Au/Si (50 nm Au on Si) with light manual pressure to ensure conformal contact; lift to transfer SAMs.<cite id="d01ab6fc-1">Inking for 30 s in 0.5 mg/mL alkanethiol in ethanol, drying, and conformal contact printing on Au/Si with manual pressure</cite>.
- Masking and etch transfer: Patterned SAMs resist wet etching to transfer features into underlying metal layers; unmasked regions are etched away, leaving μCP-defined metal features.<cite id="d01ab6fc-3">The structured SAM acts as an etch mask during wet chemical etching and the pattern is transfer into the gold layer</cite>.
- Fidelity control: Keep printing times short and pressures modest for micron-scale channels to avoid deformation; verify stamp feature size and substrate contact with optical/MRI alignment and backside registration strategies.<cite id="df68d5dd-2">Minimal printing time at atmospheric pressure produced best resolution in channel patterns</cite><cite id="df68d5dd-3">Backside alignment methods are commonly used when stamps are optically quasi-transparent</cite>.
- Biofunctionalization: After SAM printing, incubate with ECM proteins (e.g., fibronectin) to promote cell adhesion on patterned islands; passivate unpatterned areas (e.g., BSA) to suppress nonspecific binding.<cite id="d01ab6fc-4">Stamps incubated with fibronectin and pressed onto substrates; passivation with BSA</cite><cite id="d01ab6fc-0">RGD peptide headgroups promote cell attachment and can replace conventional passivation chemistries</cite>.
- Stretchable interconnects: Use μCP stamp transfer or successive droplet deposition to pattern liquid-metal lines on elastomeric carriers; oxidation layers stabilize deposited features during circuit formation.<cite id="df68d5dd-1">Stamp printing and successive droplet deposition of liquid metal enable arbitrary planar patterns including intersecting and closed-loop circuits; oxide layers preserve deposited droplet shapes</cite>.

Summary
Microcontact printing is a robust, low-cost, and conformal soft-lithography method that transfers molecular inks—most notably alkanethiols to form SAM masks and biofunctional interfaces—from PDMS stamps to substrates, enabling micron-to-submicron patterning on planar and curved surfaces for electronics, photonics, microfluidics, and bioelectronics.<cite id="3cf6ed03-0">Soft lithography and its contact-transfer μCP method enable high-resolution microstructures on curved and planar substrates for flexible electronics, microfluidics, biosensors, and optics</cite><cite id="d01ab6fc-0">μCP transfers alkanethiols from PDMS stamps to Au/Ag to pattern SAMs that control protein adsorption and cells, and serve as etch-protective masks</cite><cite id="3cf6ed03-2">PDMS stamps replicated from masters are inked and contacted to transfer molecules into patterned layers; the technique is attractive because of simplicity, biocompatibility, speed, and low cost</cite>. While alignment, multilayer stacking, and stamp-feature transfer fidelity remain practical challenges, stamp engineering, reactive chemistry, and integration with standard microfabrication and soft-biointerface workflows have broadened μCP’s utility across devices from stretchable interconnects to organ-on-chip interfaces.<cite id="3cf6ed03-0">Soft lithography faces alignment accuracy and multilayer stacking challenges that require improvement</cite><cite id="df68d5dd-3">Pre-strained elastomeric stamps enable 800 nm pattern transfer via two-step μCP</cite><cite id="df68d5dd-1">μCP enables clean-room free deposition of liquid metals for complex interconnect patterns</cite><cite id="df68d5dd-4">Thin-film microcontact printed PDMS layers bond multilayer structures in PDMS–parylene devices for organ-on-chip integration</cite>.

Title: Revolutionizing wearable technology: advanced fabrication techniques for body-conformable electronics
Snippet: Soft lithography is a micro-and nanoscale 3D structure fabrication technology that utilizes flexible materials (e.g., polymers or elastomers) as stamps to form micron-or nanoscale patterns on a substrate through physical contact or chemical interaction in a direct or indirect manner 87,88 . Based on the basic concept, various soft lithography techniques have been developed, including contact transfer-based microcontact printing (μCP), contact transfer microtransfer molding (μTM), solvent-assisted capillary micromolding (SAMIM), and capillary micromolding techniques (MIMIC) that rely on capillary forces. These techniques are widely used for fabricating 3D structures. Soft lithography offers significant advantages for flexible electronics fabrication. It provides cost benefits, particularly in low-volume or lab-scale applications. Moreover, soft lithography allows the fabrication of complex and high-resolution microstructures on non-planar substrates and is relatively simple to execute. The realization of high-resolution patterning at low cost is crucial for the further development of body-comfort electronics. These technologies find extensive applications in microfluidic chips, biosensors, nanoelectronic devices, and optical components 89 . However, there are certain challenges associated with soft lithography that need to be addressed. The low accuracy of alignment, which relies on manual operation, is an area that requires improvement. Additionally, accurately stacking multiple layers in the fabrication of multilayer structures remains a challenge that needs to be overcome in this technology. Soft lithography technology has unveiled significant potential and prospective applications within the micro-and nano-manufacturing domain. In biomedical applications, the deployment of flexible biosensors and microfluidic devices is anticipated to catalyze the evolution of personalized healthcare and the proliferation of point-of-care diagnostic methodologies. 

Microcontact printing (μCP) μCP, the most mature soft lithography process, is a method used for patterning molecular ink onto a surface with an elastic stamp. In this process, the desired molecules such as metals and nanoparticles are applied to the stamp, which is then brought into conformal contact with the substrate.

Title: Micro and Nanofabrication methods to control cell-substrate interactions and cell behavior: A review from the tissue engineering perspective
Snippet: Micro and nanostructures can be constructed using soft lithography and employ polymers such as polydimethylsiloxane, PDMS as templates (soft lithography) or stamps (microcontact printing) (Fig. 2cee). Soft lithography has the advantages of low cost and ease and is frequently used in the production of micropatterned substrates from various materials [16,58,60,67,68]. Curved surfaces can also be used successfully due to the flexibility of PDMS while photolithography is not suitable for such surfaces [69]. Microcontact printing is a method similar to image transfer like a regular stamp and ink. It is used to pattern molecules on a surface for cell behavior and protein adsorption applications [61,62]. In microcontact printing, PDMS is used to produce a stamp by replica molding. Then the stamp is inked to adsorb cells, proteins and other molecules to transfer them onto the substrate. After the stamp is pressed, the solvent is evaporated, and molecules are transferred, the stamp is removed revealing the patterns. Microcontact printing can be used for large areas, and multiple copies of the patterns can be obtained by a single stamp by applying it repeatedly. High aspect ratio patterns is not possible with this technique.

Title: Soft Lithography, a Tool to Address Single-Objects Investigations
Snippet: Soft-lithography emerged in the early 90's as a technique based on the use of an elastomer material named polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS). This polymer can be poured onto a siliconbased master with micro-or nanostructures made by photolithography or electron beam lithography respectively, to obtain a PDMS replication of the master's structures. The corresponding PDMS stamp can then be inked with a molecule and put in contact with a target surface to transfer the molecules into a patterned layer. This is what we call microcontact printing (Kumar & Whitesides, 1993;Xia & Whitesides, 1998). The major advantages of microcontact printing are that the contact with the surface is made in a very gentle manner, so the bioentities are transferred without damaging them. The flexibility of the PDMS stamp and the ability to achieve conformal contact between the stamp and the surface enables high-resolution patterning on both planar and non-planar surfaces. Areas greater than 50 cm² have been patterned by microcontact printing (Xia et al., 1996). So this technique is suitable for large-area micro-or nanopatterning, and is attractive because of its simplicity, biocompatibility, speed, and low cost. Directed Capillary Assembly is another interesting technique that has received constant interest throughout the years. This technique was first introduced by Denkov et al. in the 90's. At that time, their objective was to produce photonic band gap materials based on the compact assembly of dielectric colloids (silica beads). The method relied on the direct evaporation of a droplet of a colloidal solution on a surface and was called Capillary Force Assembly (CFA). The nanoparticles dragged by the convective flux in the droplet were forced to assemble on the surface close to the liquid meniscus. A few years later, the group of Alivisatos (Klein et al., 1996) showed how this method could be combined with topographic patterns in order to control the position of the assembly as well as the shape of the nanoparticles' patterns and this was called "Lithography Guided Capillary Force Assembly".

Title: Highly elastic conductive polymeric MEMS
Snippet: To show the feasibility of the process, we prepared different mixtures of conductive particles added to a very soft PDMS base material. Conductivity is attained by use of carbon black powder, MWCNTs, and silver flakes. However, to achieve conductivity, various other admixtures are conceivable and do not impair the fabrication process itself. The electrical properties of these three different mixtures are measured with a special focus on conductivity under strain. As a possible application for the process, we finally fabricated a highly elastic strain gauge, and we showed the results of the electrical measurements under high strain.

Microstructuring of conductive PDMS is achieved by micromolding, where a negative mold of the desired structure is used to define the geometry of the polymer. This negative mold is frequently made of a thick film resist coated on a silicon or glass substrate. Alternatively, molding microstructures directly etched into silicon or glass is the method of choice. In both cases, conductive PDMS is poured onto the micromold and excess composite is scraped off using a blade or a similar tool. Nonconductive PDMS is then poured on top of the conductive PDMS as an insulating carrier layer. After cross-linking, the PDMS carrier layer can be peeled off the mold, along with the conductive layer. This method is often referred to as soft lithography. Another way to pattern conductive PDMS is microcontact printing. In this case, a micro fabricated printing mold (e.g., poly(methyl methacrylate)), is used to transfer a thin layer of conductive PDMS from a carrier to a glass slide. In a subsequent step, nonconductive PDMS is poured on top of the imprinted conductive PDMS. After curing, the PDMS layer can again be peeled off, along with the printed microstructures.

Both micromolding approaches, either by using structured resist or etched structures in a substrate, have their downsides. During removal of excess polymer, the master mold is often damaged or scratched, and it is difficult to thoroughly separate small pitched microstructures. In the case of microcontact printing, a printing mold has to be fabricated and only thin layers of conductive PDMS can be transferred

Title: Microfabrication of polydimethylsiloxane–parylene hybrid microelectrode array integrated into a multi-organ-on-a-chip
Snippet: The microfabrication technique employed for the device [Fig. 1(d)] is the typical multilayer soft lithography that combines soft lithography with the capability to bond multiple patterned layers of PDMS. 64,65) Figure 4(a) shows the schematic of the detailed fabrication procedure for the entire device. In this process, a uniform PDMS mortar (uncured PDMS) was achieved using a thin-film PDMS microcontact printing method 66,67) and was used for bonding each layer. Prior to the bonding process, the perfusion layer was cut partially to accommodate the contact pads of MEA as shown in Fig. 1(a). The entire device bonded to the glass substrate was finally cured in a convection oven at 80 °C for 12 h.

Title: Nanofabrication of Nonfouling Surfaces for Micropatterning of Cell and Microtissue
Snippet: The microcontact printing method [108,109] is based on the pattern transfer of the material of interest from the PDMS stamp onto the substrate surface. The PDMS stamp is prepared by fabricating it from a master (typically microfabricated in silicon) having relief structures in photoresist on its surface (for details, see ref. [105]). Photolithography is used for the fabrication of masters in preparing PDMS stamps. Many of the studies involving the patterning of proteins and cells using microcontact printing have used selfassembled monolayers (SAMs) of alkanethiols on gold. As shown in Figure 10(b), the material of interest (e.g., an alkanethiol) is transferred from the PDMS stamp onto the substrate surface (e.g., gold or silver). The bare areas of substrate surface that the PDMS stamp has not touched can be exposed to another coating material (e.g., another kind of alkanethiol). The microcontact printing provides the patterning of self-assembled monolayers, and the resulting control over the adsorption of adhesive proteins facilitates the patterning of cells on substrates [108][109][110][111][112]. 

Chemicals to form SAMs typically have a chemical formula of Y(CH 2 )nX where Y is the anchor and X is the headgroup. Title: Development of Nanowire Patterning Process Using Microcontact Printing

Title: Robust and Multifunctional Liquid-Metal Embedded Elastomers for Ultrastretchable Electronics: a Short Review
Snippet: Microcontact printing is an inexpensive and clean-room free technique for depositing soft and conductive inks on a soft substrate. There are two primary methods to pattern liquid metals using micro-contact printing: 1-Stamp printing or entire transferring of ink using a topographical stamp, and 2-successive deposition of individual droplets of liquid metal with a hemispherical print head. In contrast to stencil lithography and injecting filling, microcontact printing (stamp printing and successive deposition) can be used to create circuits with any planar pattern with intersecting and closed-loop circuit features [28,34]. 

The process benefits from the oxide layer, which preserves the shape of the deposited droplets of liquid metal.

Title: Time and pressure dependent deformation of microcontact printed channels fabricated using self-assembled monolayers of alkanethiol on gold
Snippet: Abstract In this work, the replication-based microcontact printing method has been presented to study the deformation effect of different printing times and printing pressures on the microcontact printed structures. Cost-effective microcontact printing channels of self-assembled monolayers of alkanethiol have been prepared on gold surface. The alkanethiol inking the polydimethylsiloxanes stamp effectively forms the self-assembled monolayers on the noble gold surface that protects the metal against etchant solution and thereby forms channel-like structures. To address the deformation issue, variations in the printing time in the range of 30 s–60 min and the printing pressure ranging from 840 to 4200 Pa have been studied. The estimation of differing the channel width and channel space with varying printing time and pressure shows the best resolution structures printed under minimal printing time at atmospheric pressure.

Title: Cost-effective fabrication of submicron-scale patterns enabled by microcontact printing with a pre-strained soft elastomeric stamp
Snippet: Fig. 5 presents the results of microcontact printing using the released Ecoex stamp. The replicated pattern on the Ecoex stamp, as shown in Fig. 5a, features a line pattern with an initial width and gap of approximately 4 mm, reduced from the original 10 mm line pattern according to the pre-strain of 3.0. We spincoated the PR layer on top of this and dened the pattern on a prepared Si substrate by microcontact printing. Fig. 5b exhibits the optical images of the successfully dened PR pattern with a width of 4 mm. Additionally, to achieve submicrometer scale PR patterns, we used a stamp with a line pattern width of 800 nm, as shown in the optical micrograph in Fig. 5c. The line pattern of 800 nm in the stamp was obtained by  shrinking a pattern originally obtained through I-line photolithography with a width of 2 mm according to the pre-strain of 3.0. Introducing the proposed fabrication process, we successfully achieved 800 nm line patterns, via microcontact printing, as shown in Fig. 5d. The quasi-opacity of Ecoex in the visible range poses challenges for typically used top-view optical alignment. However, alternative alignment methods, particularly those utilizing the backside of the substrate, have been well established and widely adopted in photolithography processes. 20 These processes commonly use wafer substrates, silicon with high transmission in the infrared range, and glass or quartz with high transmission in both the visible and infrared ranges.

Title: Distinct roles of nonmuscle myosin II isoforms for establishing tension and elasticity during cell morphodynamics
Snippet: Micropatterned substrates were prepared using the microcontact printing technique (Mrksich and Whitesides, 1996). Briefly, a master structure, which serves as a negative mold for the silicon stamp was produced by direct laser writing (Anscombe, 2010) and the stamp was molded from the negative using Sylgard 184 (Dow Corning #105989377). The stamp-pattern resembles a sequence of crosses with different intersections, a bar width of 5 mm and edge length of 45-65 mm. The pattern was either transferred using gold-thiol chemistry (Mrksich et al., 1997) or direct microcontact printing (Fritz and Bastmeyer, 2013). When using gold-thiol chemistry, the stamp was inked with a 1.5 mM solution of octadecylmercaptan (Sigma Aldrich #O1858) in ethanol and pressed onto the goldcoated coverslip, forming a self-assembled monolayer at the protruding parts of the stamp. For the subsequent passivation of uncoated areas, 2.5 mM solution of hexa(ethylene glycol)-terminated alkanethiol (ProChimia Surfaces #TH-001-m11.n6) in ethanol was used. Micropatterned coverslips were functionalized with a solution of 10 mg ml À1 FN from human plasma (Sigma Aldrich #F1056) for 1 hr at room temperature. For direct microcontact printing, stamps were incubated for 10 min with a solution of 10 mg ml À1 FN and pressed onto uncoated a coverslip. Passivation was carried out using a BSA-Solution of 10 mg ml À1 in PBS for backfilling of the coverslip at room temperature for 1 hr.

snippet.text: Fig. 5 presents the results of microcontact printing using the released Ecoex stamp. The replicated pattern on the Ecoex stamp, as shown in Fig. 5a, features a line pattern with an initial width and gap of approximately 4 mm, reduced from the original 10 mm line pattern according to the pre-strain of 3.0. We spincoated the PR layer on top of this and dened the pattern on a prepared Si substrate by microcontact printing. Fig. 5b exhibits the optical images of the successfully dened PR pattern with a width of 4 mm. Additionally, to achieve submicrometer scale PR patterns, we used a stamp with a line pattern width of 800 nm, as shown in the optical micrograph in Fig. 5c. The line pattern of 800 nm in the stamp was obtained by  shrinking a pattern originally obtained through I-line photolithography with a width of 2 mm according to the pre-strain of 3.0. Introducing the proposed fabrication process, we successfully achieved 800 nm line patterns, via microcontact printing, as shown in Fig. 5d. The quasi-opacity of Ecoex in the visible range poses challenges for typically used top-view optical alignment. However, alternative alignment methods, particularly those utilizing the backside of the substrate, have been well established and widely adopted in photolithography processes. 20 These processes commonly use wafer substrates, silicon with high transmission in the infrared range, and glass or quartz with high transmission in both the visible and infrared ranges.
